Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by ghosts. Whoever committed the murders had a physical body and escaped by physical means. But how? Fortunately, there is only one way to reason through this question, and it must bring us to a definite answer. Let us consider every possible exit in turn. Clearly, when the group came upstairs, the killers were in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or at least in the next room. We therefore need to look for exits only from those two rooms. The police have thoroughly exposed the floors, ceilings, and walls. No secret passage could have escaped their attention. Still, I did not rely on their eyes; I examined everything myself. There were no secret exits. Both doors into the hallway were firmly locked, with the keys on the inside. Now consider the chimneys. Though they are of normal width for eight or ten feet above the fireplaces, farther up they narrow so much that even a large cat could not pass through. Since escape by any of these routes was absolutely impossible, only the windows remain. No one could have escaped through the front-room windows without being seen by the crowd in the street. The murderers must therefore have used the back-room windows. Having reached this conclusion so clearly, we cannot reject it simply because it appears impossible. Our task is to show that these apparent ‘impossibilities’ are actually possible.

“There are two windows in the bedroom. No furniture blocks the first, which is completely visible. The lower part of the other is hidden by the head of the large, heavy bed, pushed right against it. The first window was found securely fastened inside. Those who tried to raise it could not move it, however hard they pulled. A large hole had been drilled into the left side of its frame, and a very thick nail had been driven into it almost to the head. When the other window was examined, a similar nail was found in the same position. A forceful attempt to raise that window also failed. The police were then entirely convinced that no one had escaped through either window. They consequently thought it unnecessary to remove the nails and open them.

“My own examination was more thorough, for exactly the reason I have just explained. I knew that here, at these windows, everything that appeared impossible had to be shown possible in fact.

February had begun, and Anne, after a month in Bath, was becoming exceedingly anxious for tidings of Uppercross and Lyme. She wished to learn far more than Mary had told her. Three weeks had passed without any news. All she knew was that Henrietta had returned home, while Louisa, though said to be recovering rapidly, remained at Lyme. One evening, when her thoughts were dwelling earnestly on them all, a letter thicker than Mary generally sent was brought to her; and, to heighten both her delight and surprise, it came with Admiral and Mrs Croft’s compliments.

The Crofts must have come to Bath! Here was something to interest her. Her heart inclined towards them most naturally.

“What is this?” exclaimed Sir Walter. “The Crofts are in Bath? Those Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought for you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, sir.”

“Oh! Such letters make convenient passports. They procure an introduction. I should, however, have called upon Admiral Croft in any event. I understand what is owing to my tenant.”

Anne could attend no longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion fared, so completely did her letter occupy her. It had been started several days before.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

I offer no excuse for not writing, since I know how little anyone values letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to trouble yourself about Uppercross, where, as you know perfectly well, there is scarcely anything to write of. Our Christmas has been very dull; Mr and Mrs Musgrove have not given a single dinner party during the whole holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anybody. At least the holidays have finally ended: I think no children ever enjoyed such lengthy ones. Certainly I never did. Yesterday the house emptied, apart from the young Harvilles; but you will be astonished to learn that they have never returned home. Mrs Harville must be a strange mother to spare them for so long. I cannot understand it. In my opinion they are not at all agreeable children; yet Mrs Musgrove appears as fond of them as of her grandchildren, if not fonder. What frightful weather we have been having! Perhaps you scarcely notice it in Bath, with those fine pavements; in the country it matters considerably. Since January’s second week not a soul has visited me except Charles Hayter, who has been coming much more often than I desire. Between ourselves, I think it most unfortunate that Henrietta did not stay at Lyme as long as Louisa; she would then have been somewhat out of his reach.

The next day was fixed for producing the proof, lest delay should give our honor a chill. Drummle duly appeared with a brief, polite statement in Estella’s handwriting, confirming that she had had the honor of dancing with him several times. This left me no choice but to express regret that I had been “carried away by a heat of feeling which,” and generally to withdraw, as indefensible, the suggestion that I was available to be challenged anywhere. Drummle and I then spent an hour snorting at each other while the Grove contradicted everything indiscriminately, after which the advancement of friendly relations was declared astonishing.

I describe this lightly, but it was far from light to me. I cannot adequately convey the pain of imagining Estella showing favor to a contemptible, awkward, sullen fool, so far beneath even the average. To this day I believe that some pure spark of generosity and selflessness in my love made me unable to bear the thought of her lowering herself to that cur. I would doubtless have been miserable whoever she favored, but a worthier man would have caused distress of a different kind and degree.

It was easy to discover, and I soon did, that Drummle had begun pursuing her closely and that she permitted it. Before long he was constantly following her, and he and I encountered one another every day. He persisted with dull determination, and Estella kept him pursuing her: sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes almost flattering him, sometimes openly showing contempt, at one moment treating him as an intimate, at another barely remembering his identity.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had named him, was accustomed to lying in wait and possessed the patience of his kind. He also had a fool’s confidence in his wealth and the importance of his family, which sometimes served him well, almost substituting for concentration and firm purpose. So the Spider, stubbornly watching Estella, waited out many brighter insects and would often uncurl himself and drop down at exactly the right moment.

At a particular Assembly Ball in Richmond—most places held Assembly Balls in those days—Estella had eclipsed every other beauty. The blundering Drummle hovered around her so persistently, and she tolerated him so readily, that I decided to speak to her about him. I took the next opportunity, when she was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave and waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home.
